item.title: Is It Time for This 95-Year-Old Pianist to Quit?
item.description:
“I never thought about retiring. It never occurred to me.”

At 95 years old, Lily Friedman is wondering how long she can continue performing and teaching.

“I think you have to have some meaning. You can’t just exist.”

Supported by

Exit strategy

Her vision and hearing are deteriorating, but she still wants to feel like she’s on top.

By Sarah Kramer

Visuals by Shuran Huang

Exit Strategy is a series about people confronting the challenges of retirement, told in their own words.

Lily Friedman has had a rollicking career as a pianist, a performer and a teacher.

But after more than seven decades of working, in the quiet moments a thought now nags at her.

All these famous guys say they stop while they’re “on top,” and I don’t know how you know when you’re on the top. Because I don’t feel I’m on top yet.

Has she already reached the top, and begun to decline? She doesn’t want to go out with her students dissatisfied, or her performance faltering.

Then again, she doesn’t want to stop at all.

Knowing when, how and whether to retire has long vexed people reaching the ends of their careers. By 2030, 74 million Americans will be over 65, and in that season of life when retirement usually begins, compared with 49 million a decade ago.

With the country becoming older as the baby boomer generation ages, the number of Americans on that precipice — as they reckon with their professional desires, new limitations and financial needs — will soon grow larger than it ever has been.

While some welcome these years and have planned ahead for them, Ms. Friedman is guided solely by her passion to keep playing.

You’re really laying your soul bare, is what you’re trying to do, and hoping that they get the same message, that they feel something.

As the story goes, Ms. Friedman asked her parents for piano lessons at the age of 5, and she has been playing since. After she graduated from Juilliard in 1952, postcards started appearing in her mailbox with teaching opportunities, and her student roster grew. At one point, Ms. Friedman played concerts regularly and juggled as many as 50 students. Now she has fewer than a dozen.

I had students and they just kept coming, and now it’s down. It’s dwindled and dwindled. The kids have grown and gone to college, gone away, and the adults are getting older.

The lessons are tiring. If I play for an hour, an hour and a half, I am tired. And I can lie down when I think it’ll be 20 minutes. Two and a half hours later, I wake up. I am very pissed about that.

When I can’t see the notes, I wonder if I should stop teaching. I say I need a telescope and I joke about it, but I wonder if I should.

But this is also the teacher whose enthusiasm for playing inspired her surgeon, after he operated on her gallbladder, to become her student. And there’s Yujin Kim, a 38-year-old veterinary professor, who commutes two hours each way, weekly, to study with Ms. Friedman in her apartment on the Upper West Side of Manhattan.

During their first session last year, Ms. Kim recalled, Ms. Friedman told her to slightly change the angle of her pinkie. “That totally changes the sound quality, and she just knew,” Ms. Kim said. “That is why I feel I’m listened to by her.”

For Ms. Friedman, the losses have come incrementally.

First it was stepping down about 12 years ago as the artistic director of Summer Trios, a chamber music organization that she had co-founded. Ms. Friedman was taking care of her partner at the end of his life and found herself unable to do both.

Then it was parting with her red Mini Cooper. She gave it to her grandson after her sons forbade her from taking the wheel; she was 92.

And then it was her annual New Year’s Day fund-raiser for Summer Trios at her apartment, a daylong music celebration, complete with her homemade stuffed cabbage. Last year, she no longer had the stamina to organize it.

Perhaps the biggest transition of recent years unfolded after a surgery in 2022, when she started needing both a cane (she chose a red one with red rhinestones) and a round-the-clock caregiver, covered by her insurance.

Now her vision and hearing are waning.

Thirty five years ago when Ms. Friedman established Summer Trios, which offers workshops for amateur chamber musicians, things were different. It was an era when Ms. Friedman survived on ice cream, Hershey bars and little sleep as she kept Summer Trios running.

It is still going strong. In June, nearly 100 participants attended during the two-week program, at Franklin & Marshall College in Lancaster, Pa. Many still remember that first summer there, and Ms. Friedman is still the draw.

This year, she mentored a few groups and played Brahms’s Piano Quartet No. 3 in C minor (Op. 60) for her faculty performance.

Oh, it was an ordeal. It was awful as far as I was concerned. I mean, it might have sounded OK to the others, but I literally couldn’t see. And I was so focused I don’t even remember who I’m playing with, who the cellist was.

Everybody thought it was fabulous, but it was not good.

For her second performance, she was more prepared and rested, and armed with enlarged sheet music. Even so, it was not easy.

They recorded every faculty concert, and I looked at mine and I’m stiff because I couldn’t see, even on the large copy. It was very tense and I can’t always hear the high violin notes.

I don’t know if any of that can be fixed.

She would later learn that some mentees had complained about her hearing, and, for the second year in a row, there was a cake celebrating Ms. Friedman at the reception after the performance, which felt a bit like a retirement party.

And then there was the composition she played. It had been the first piece of chamber music Ms. Friedman and Chris Lee, her collaborator of close to 50 years, had performed together. He had suggested that they play it again this year.

The complaints, the composition, the retirement party of sorts; it all seemed to be subtly hinting at something. Should this be her last summer?

Nobody said anything like that. But the implication was sort of there.

I don’t know if I’ll go next year. We’ll have to see what happens.

Ms. Friedman still has many pieces she wants to learn, and others that she has nearly mastered. One in particular.

Wow. I worked on it. I played it every day.

I was so upset about Ukraine, because my father was from Ukraine, that I dug up this piece by Beethoven. It’s famous in the repertoire as being very, very difficult. It’s a 45-minute piece.

And then I don’t play it for a month and come back to it and there’s still some more there. There’s something I didn’t get the first time.

It’s Opus 111. It starts very angry, and then the second movement, it is so, so calming and so beautiful. I’m almost crying.

Nobody ever plays Opus 111, rarely.

After playing Opus 111, she feels like she’s broken up with someone, she said, because she can’t believe it’s over.

Ms. Friedman wants others to hear it.

So, she has set her sights on one more solo concert. Maybe then she will feel like she is going out on top.

I want a real venue, you know?

Last week, Ms. Friedman turned 95. She celebrated with a big family dinner and a canoe trip down the Housatonic River. And she has begun calling around, looking for a recital hall where she can perform again.

item.title: Target Apologizes and Drops Halloween Costume Criticized as Racist
item.description:
Target apologized on Monday and said it had stopped selling a children’s Halloween costume after facing widespread criticism that the design evoked racist stereotypes of Black people.

The product listing on Target’s website, which appears to have been deleted, showed a circus clown costume in orange and black, with accessories including gloves, a top hat and a mask shaped like a grinning mouth with large teeth.

Critics said that these features, in addition to a promotional image that appeared to show a Black child modeling the costume, mirrored caricatures from Jim Crow-era minstrel shows.

Target, the Minneapolis-based big box retailer with around 2,000 U.S. stores, said in a statement that it had stopped selling the costume and would look into how it had gone on sale.

“As a company, we know we got this wrong, and we are deeply sorry,” it said.

“The costume is offensive and should never have been part of our assortment,” the statement continued, adding: “We know this is especially hurtful for our Black guests, team members and partners.”

Minstrel shows were a form of 19th-century American theater built around caricatures of Black people and culture. Performers, who were usually white, wore blackface and enacted these caricatures for predominantly white audiences.

Dong-hwan Lee, a professor at the Gyeongin National University of Education in South Korea who specializes in American culture and has written on minstrel shows, said that selling such a product “reduces Black individuals to contemptible, clownish figures.”

Shomane Touré, the founder of Afrocentric Films Collaborative, a group based in Oakland, Calif., that promotes Black culture, said that Target seemed to have neglected to consider how the product was presented.

“Target appears to have overlooked these historical implications by choosing to market a costume worn by a Black child in a manner that can be interpreted as reinforcing a longstanding racial stereotype,” Mr. Touré said in an emailed statement.

Target did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.

Other major brands have dropped products criticized as racist. During Black History Month in 2019, Gucci apologized and pulled a sweater that had an opening for the mouth with bright red lips that were widely denounced as evoking blackface.

Target, which has struggled financially while losing ground to rival Walmart, was at the center of controversy over its Pride Month marketing campaign in 2023. That campaign drew anger from some on the political right, including some customers who demonstrated confrontational behavior in stores, the company said. After Target removed some merchandise in response, some L.G.B.T.Q. advocacy groups criticized Target for appearing to cave to pressure.

item.title: China Pushes Back After Trump Tightens the Screws on Iran
item.description:
China lashed out at the Trump administration’s new sanctions campaign against Iran on Tuesday, warning that it would defend its interests and accusing the United States of disrupting the global financial order.

The reaction set the stage for renewed friction between the world’s superpowers.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday outlined plans to “sever every economic lifeline” to Iran, targeting a constellation of players that continue to provide the country with a financial lifeline. But the administration appeared to tread carefully around China, by far the largest customer of its most valuable export: oil.

The U.S. list of more than 60 brokers, companies and ships subject to sanctions included more than a dozen small companies from Hong Kong and China. Conspicuously absent were heavyweights in China’s financial system — a sign, some experts said, that Washington was reluctant to jeopardize a fragile truce with China.

Beijing nevertheless responded forcefully. China would “take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own rights and interests,” Lin Jian, a spokesman for the foreign ministry, said at a news briefing on Tuesday.

Chinese state media went further. An editorial cartoon in China News portrayed the Statue of Liberty as a drug user with needles protruding from one arm, describing Washington’s use of sanctions as “an addiction.”

The confrontational reaction underscored a dilemma for the Trump administration. Beijing has long defied American sanctions and continued to buy Iranian oil. At the same time, China supplied Tehran with raw materials and technology that support its economy and military. Yet, nearly six months into a war with Iran, the United States has shown little appetite for opening another economic front with an increasingly retaliatory China.

The timing is particularly delicate. China’s top leader, Xi Jinping, is expected to travel to the United States next month to meet with President Trump to continue talks aimed at stabilizing the countries’ relationship.

On Monday, when he was asked why the administration had not targeted Chinese banks, Mr. Bessent said only that “quiet diplomacy” was the best form of engagement. He did vow at one point to still penalize a large international financial institution, though he did not offer specifics. To some analysts, Mr. Bessent’s failure to call out China amounted to a tacit acknowledgment that preserving the truce with China may, for now, outweigh the benefits of taking more aggressive action against Iran.

Washington “has been extremely reluctant to go after China,” said Daniel Tannebaum, a former Treasury Department official during the George W. Bush administration and now a partner at Oliver Wyman, a consulting firm. “I don’t think that changes today, especially at a time when China has more leverage than the United States does.”

For decades, the United States has exploited its central position in the global financial system to isolate adversaries like Iran and North Korea, threatening to exclude companies and banks from conducting transactions in dollars if they do business with sanctioned entities. Successive rounds of sanctions have largely left Iran cut off from the global financial system, but they have failed to incapacitate its economy.

But more recently, China has shown it is willing to use its own economic choke points. During the bruising trade war of the past year, Beijing restricted access to critical minerals and used its control over supply chains against American companies as leverage.

China agreed last year to temporarily postpone controls on exports of rare earth minerals as part of a thaw in relations with the United States. That one-year reprieve is set to lapse weeks after Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump are scheduled to meet.

That leverage has raised the potential cost of confronting Beijing over Iran, even as China has become critical to Tehran’s ability to withstand American pressure.

Since the United States and Israel launched their attack on Iran on Feb. 28, Washington has sanctioned more than 400 companies, people and ships tied to Iran from countries including Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, China and Hong Kong.

It has added more than 1,000 entities to its sanctions list since the start of Mr. Trump’s second term, effectively cutting them off from the dollar, according to an analysis by The New York Times. The targets have included Chinese shipping companies and oil refiners.

Yet, Iranian oil has continued to flow to China.

Large quantities are now sitting aboard ships and in storage tanks around the Malacca Strait, the South China Sea and near Chinese ports, according to Muyu Xu, a senior oil analyst at Kpler, an industry data provider.

Data from Kpler shows that China has received around 1.2 million barrels of oil a day from Iran so far in 2026, only slightly less than the same period last year. Up-to-date volumes are difficult to measure because ships have become increasingly skilled at evading detection, Ms. Xu said.

China’s three national state-controlled oil giants have avoided buying Iranian crude because of their extensive ties to Western banks. But privately owned Chinese refiners known as “teapots” have bought Iranian oil at steep discounts and turned it into gasoline and diesel for the domestic market.

Those companies can be especially difficult for Washington to pressure. Many have few international transactions that the Treasury Department can target by restricting access to the dollar through global banks. Instead, they are believed to conduct much of their trade in Chinese currency or cryptocurrencies.

The trade has also developed elaborate methods for shielding ships and cargoes from Western sanctions. Iranian oil is frequently transported to waters off Malaysia, where cargos are transferred between vessels before continuing to Chinese ports.

In April, the United States targeted a handful of Chinese teapot refineries, including Hengli Petrochemical Refinery. One of Iran’s biggest customers, the refinery was found to have purchased billions of dollars of Iranian crude from the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, which wields considerable military, political and economic clout in Iran.

Still, even if the U.S. Treasury Department does not take overt measures against big Chinese banks, international banks might start curtailing business with them, according to Han Lin, the China country director of The Asia Group, an American consulting firm. Big banks are wary about incurring the wrath of American regulators.

The big international banks “will become much more conservative about engaging in any transactions” with any Chinese financial institutions, he said.

Washington has confronted China over Iranian oil before. Around 2012, during the administration of President Barack Obama, American diplomats pressed China and other countries to wind down purchases of Iranian crude, which were then conducted more openly.

Around that time, the United States also put sanctions on Bank of Kunlun, a Chinese financial institution owned by China National Petroleum Corp., over its ties to Iran and for doing business with Iranian banks already under sanctions.

But the Trump administration has stopped short of imposing the kind of sanctions on major financial institutions that could fundamentally disrupt Beijing’s economic relationship with Tehran.

“We have not in recent years demonstrated a willingness to run the risk of undermining our economic standing” in exchange for pushing Chinese banks away from Iran, said Richard Nephew, a former official in the Obama administration who helped negotiate the Iran nuclear agreement.

There are powerful reasons for that caution. Mr. Nephew pointed to Washington’s 2018 sanctions against Oleg Deripaska and Rusal, the Russian giant that was then the world’s second-largest aluminum producer. Aluminum markets went haywire at the prospect of a major source of global supply being cut off.

Targeting systemically important Chinese banks or companies could produce a shock on an entirely different scale.

“You could find markets going nuts,” Mr. Nephew said. “You could find companies going nuts. You can find insurance companies going nuts, banks going nuts.”

Murphy Zhao contributed reporting from Hong Kong.
